frames.narration: A client searches. The index is split into 8 shards, each holding a slice of the documents. The coordinator cannot know which shards hold matches, so it asks all of them (two are drawn here).
Each shard searches its own segments and returns its top 10 hits, as ids and scores: 80 entries in all. The coordinator merges them and keeps the best 10.

Shard 2 hits a garbage-collection pause: 200 ms extra. The coordinator needs every answer, so the whole query takes about 230 ms. With 8 shards, 4.3% of queries meet a slow shard; with 32 shards it is 15.2%.
Fix the tail: send the request to a replica of shard 2 as well and use the first answer. A slow copy no longer matters unless both are slow, so p99 drops to 32 ms.
Break it: a user jumps to results 10,001 to 10,010. Every shard must return its own top 10,010, so 8 shards send 80,080 entries to the coordinator to show 10.
Cursor paging fixes it: the client sends the sort value of the last hit it saw (search_after), and each shard returns only the next 10 after it. Work stays flat however deep the user goes.

One more trap: if shard 1 holds 3 times the data of the others, it answers last every time. The median query time doubles from 32 ms to 67 ms. Latency is set by the biggest shard, so keep shards even.
